Week 2 Appendix: Speed as a Method of Rule

In its first full week back, the new administration opened a dozen fronts at once, testing whether pace alone could outrun courts, Congress, and the press.

This week—the first full week of the second Trump term—shows a systemic, multi-front assault on institutional checks rather than a single dramatic event. The dominant pattern is rapid, simultaneous executive action: mass pardons of January 6 defendants including a seditious-conspiracy leader, firing of 17+ inspectors general without statutory notice, purges of DOJ prosecutors and FBI agents tied to Trump investigations, an attempted funding freeze affecting trillions in federal spending, and an executive order challenging birthright citizenship. Immigration enforcement escalated sharply (ICE quotas, Chicago raids, Guantánamo detention plans, church/school raids), while civil service protections were undermined via mass buyout offers and Schedule F-style reclassification. Courts pushed back repeatedly—blocking the funding freeze, the birthright citizenship order, and the OMB memo—demonstrating judicial resistance even as the volume of executive action threatens to outpace institutional capacity to respond. The week reveals a strategy of overwhelming scrutiny through sheer velocity of action.

Power and Authority

  1. Trump cancelled flights for 1,600 Afghan refugees and declared a national emergency at the southern border: The president used executive power to halt refugee resettlement and declare a border emergency, expanding unilateral authority over immigration on his first days back in office. (2025-01-25)
  2. Trump pardoned or commuted sentences for about 1,500 January 6 defendants, including Oath Keepers leader Stewart Rhodes: Blanket pardons for Capitol attack participants, including a seditious-conspiracy leader, undermined accountability for a violent assault on the transfer of power. (2025-01-25)
  3. Trump invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to target immigrants labeled as gang members: Reviving a wartime-era law to justify mass immigration enforcement expands executive emergency power into a new legal domain. (2025-01-28)
  4. Trump ordered ICE to prepare a 30,000-person migrant detention facility at Guantánamo Bay naval base: Repurposing a military prison known for human rights abuses to hold civilian immigration detainees raises due process and humane-treatment concerns. (2025-01-29)
  5. Trump administration froze foreign aid except military assistance to Israel and Egypt: Halting most foreign aid without congressional input tested limits on executive control over appropriated funds and weakened diplomatic tools. (2025-01-25)
  6. Trump withdrew the United States from the Paris climate accords: Unilateral withdrawal from a major international agreement reduced U.S. commitments on global climate cooperation without legislative involvement. (2025-01-25) [single source]
  7. Trump demanded NATO members raise military spending to 5 percent of GDP: A steep new demand on allies risked destabilizing a decades-old defense alliance built to deter aggression. (2025-01-25)
  8. Trump lifted the hold on 2,000-pound bomb shipments to Israel: Reversing a prior administration's arms restriction shifted U.S. military support policy in an active conflict zone. (2025-01-25) [single source]
  9. Trump proposed relocating Gaza's 2.2 million residents to other Arab countries: A proposal to displace an entire population reflects a dramatic break from established U.S. positions on Palestinian self-determination. (2025-01-25)
  10. ICE began coordinated multi-agency immigration raids in Chicago and other cities, arresting over 950 people in one weekend: Large-scale enforcement operations, including at previously protected sites like schools and churches, escalated fear in immigrant communities and tested limits on due process. (2025-01-26)
  11. Trump administration set ICE arrest quotas of 1,200 to 1,800 people per day: Numeric enforcement targets increase pressure on agents to make arrests quickly, raising the risk of civil rights violations and wrongful detentions. (2025-01-26) [single source]
  12. US Northern Command allowed ICE to use Buckley Space Force Base in Colorado for immigration detention operations: Blending military infrastructure with civilian immigration enforcement raises questions about the militarization of domestic policy. (2025-01-27) [single source]
  13. Trump cancelled visa appointments and revoked visas for Colombian officials, then imposed 25 percent tariffs on Colombian goods after Colombia refused deportation flights: Rapid economic and diplomatic retaliation against an ally over a policy dispute strained relations and demonstrated coercive use of trade power. (2025-01-28)
  14. Pete Hegseth revoked Gen. Mark Milley's security clearance, personal security detail, and ordered a review of his rank: Stripping protections from a former joint chiefs chair who had criticized Trump signals use of military authority to punish political critics. (2025-01-29)
  15. Trump invited Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to be the first foreign leader to visit the White House: Hosting a leader wanted by the International Criminal Court signals a diplomatic stance disregarding international legal accountability. (2025-01-29)
  16. Trump signed an executive order authorizing sanctions against International Criminal Court officials: Threatening asset freezes and travel bans against an international court investigating alleged war crimes undermines global rule-of-law mechanisms. (2025-01-30)
  17. Trump ended UNRWA funding and withdrew the United States from the UN Human Rights Council: Cutting humanitarian aid to Palestinian refugees and leaving a key human rights body weakens U.S. engagement in multilateral institutions. (2025-01-30)
  18. Stephen Miller directed a purge of FBI agents who had investigated Trump, pressuring officials to produce lists for termination: A White House aide orchestrating removal of law enforcement personnel who investigated the president represents a direct attack on the independence of federal law enforcement. (2025-01-28) [single source]
  19. Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Canada and Mexico and 10 percent on China, then delayed tariffs on USMCA-covered goods and autos: Launching a broad trade war through unilateral tariff authority, later softened with selective exemptions, raised concerns about economic disruption and favoritism. (2025-01-30)
  20. Trump expanded Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency authority over federal spending systems: Granting a private citizen sweeping oversight of government payment systems raises conflicts of interest and undermines institutional independence. (2025-01-30) [single source]
